prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints tie credit to asset values and thereby amplify and propagate shocks into credit cycles and macroeconomic fluctuations

statement.case_for: My configuration has changed. In round 1 I preferred B006 with Kiyotaki, Moore and Gertler. I now propose the Kiyotaki-Moore pair. The discovery is a single, well-bounded mechanism: borrowing limits depend on collateral values, and collateral values depend on borrowing, so small shocks become large and persistent fluctuations. The mechanism explains why a pattern arises, not just that it exists, which is the criterion I value most. It is about three decades old. It has been extended and stress-tested through 2007-09 and the work that followed, and it is now part of the shared core of macro-finance and central-bank modelling. There is no maturity concern. The attribution is also the cleanest available for this ballot. Nobody in the exchange disputes Kiyotaki and Moore as the originators, and the pair avoids re-crediting the Bernanke-Gertler accelerator line. The chair asked whether Gertler's later work is a separable achievement. My honest answer is that I cannot establish this from the evidence in front of me. I recall Gertler's intermediary-frictions work with Kiyotaki and his quantitative work on unconventional policy with Karadi. The first sits close to the banking-crisis theme of the 2022 prize. The second is closer to the monetary-policy theme of B048 than to collateral amplification. This recollection comes from background knowledge, not verified sources. A third name I cannot defend cleanly should not weaken an otherwise clean prize.
statement.case_against: The 2022 prize on banks and financial crises is adjacent, and a committee could reasonably judge that macro-finance has been recently recognised. I answer that the collateral-amplification mechanism is a distinct discovery from bank runs and deposit insurance, but I accept that this is a judgement about where a boundary lies. Empirical identification of the specific collateral channel is mixed. The evidence supports amplification through credit more convincingly than the Kiyotaki-Moore mechanism in particular. The pair also leaves out Gertler and Gilchrist, whose quantitative and empirical contributions are real, so the citation has to be worded narrowly and honestly. B047 has an attribution that is as compact and a longer applied record in policy practice. Whether breadth of influence across macro, finance and policy outweighs that is a legitimate difference in judgement. I do not claim it is decisive.

responses.point: Hassler's round-1 file proposes Kiyotaki, Moore and Gertler. He ties Gertler's credit to intermediary-frictions work with Kiyotaki and to quantitative financial-friction models, and not to the accelerator papers that overlap with Bernanke's 2022 prize. He also says the overlap concern is not fully dissolved.
responses.response: I read this as his own current position. Several members, and I in round 1, answered his earlier two-name proposal. His last point is what moves me. If the overlap is not fully dissolved, the third name carries the weakest part of the case. The intermediary-frictions papers with Kiyotaki sit close to the banking theme that the 2022 prize covered, and I cannot name a paper that cleanly separates Gertler's contribution from that theme or from the accelerator. I therefore move to the pair. I still agree with his view that the citation should name collateral constraints and balance-sheet amplification and exclude bank runs and deposit insurance.

responses.point: Krusell keeps Gertler but accepts the Kiyotaki-Moore pair if the committee finds Gertler's marginal credit too entangled with Bernanke's prize. He argues that a mechanism that organised a large research programme and passed the 2008 test need not be settled in every empirical detail.
responses.response: I agree with the principle. A conceptual contribution that organised a literature can be prize-worthy without a settled identification of every channel. As an economic historian I would add a caution. Long-run evidence on credit booms and busts fits amplification through credit in general, but it does not isolate the collateral-value feedback specifically. That is why the citation should stay at the level of the mechanism and should not claim empirical settlement. On the third name, I now take the fallback you and I both described as my preferred position. I would ask whether you can name the papers that carry Gertler's separable share. The chair asked the same question, and I could not answer it with confidence.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B047 first and treats Bresnahan and Reiss as a distinct achievement, not an extension of BLP. He says the omission is a real cost of the three-name cap and should not be resolved by enlarging the prize. He also says the two-name B006 would be the alternative he would most readily support.
responses.response: This answers the question I put to the IO specialists in round 1. The Bresnahan-Reiss omission is a real cost, but it concerns a separable achievement. It does not make the BLP core unclean. I therefore treat B047 as the most credible rival on attribution. I do not agree that thematic proximity to 2022 should leave B047 clearly ahead. The collateral mechanism and the banking-crisis work are different discoveries. I accept that the proximity is a legitimate weight and is not a trivial one. I list B047 as my first alternative and no longer list B023.

responses.point: Strömberg supports a two-name Kiyotaki-Moore version as a strong alternative to B047. He argues that the 2022 overlap makes B006 less of a new step than a field with no recent recognition, and he regards the mixed identification of the collateral channel as a weaker evidentiary base than BLP's applied record.
responses.response: The chair asked for a standard that applies equally across candidates, so I will state mine. Recent recognition of an adjacent area should lead us to define the achievement more narrowly. It should not exclude it unless the new discovery is really the old one. By that standard B006 passes if the citation is limited to collateral amplification. B023 would face a similar test against the 2021, 2023 and 2024 prizes. I agree with your point on the evidentiary record, and I weigh it. Where we differ is on the relative value of a foundational mechanism and a validated toolkit. I think that is a difference in judgement and not one the facts settle.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson says Hassler's two-name framing resolves most of the attribution problem and makes B006 a stronger alternative. She asks what the empirical record says about the collateral channel itself and not about financial frictions in general. She would weigh B006 below a contribution that is both a method and a widely checked empirical practice.
responses.response: I think her question is the right test, and I cannot fully meet it. The record supports amplification through credit and balance sheets. It is less able to isolate the Kiyotaki-Moore channel. My answer is that the work supplied the structure through which later empirical and quantitative studies were designed and interpreted, and so it plays a role that is not only theoretical. I accept that this role is easier to demonstrate for BLP. For that reason I list B003, whose Mian-Sufi core is mainly empirical evidence on household credit booms, as a second alternative, and I do not claim that the empirical record gives B006 a clear lead.

uncertainties: Whether Gertler's post-accelerator work is a separable achievement or an extension of the already-honoured Bernanke-Gertler line. I could not name the papers that would settle this with confidence, and the Kiyotaki-Gertler intermediation work is close to the 2022 banking theme.
How much weight the committee should give to thematic proximity to the 2022 prize. I treat it as a reason to word the citation narrowly, but I am not sure others will agree.
Whether the collateral channel's mixed empirical record should lower B006 relative to B047, which has a longer applied record. I do not claim this is resolved.
My assessments of citations, usage and attribution come from general background knowledge, not verified sources. My expertise is in economic history and not in macro-finance or structural IO.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. No connection to Kiyotaki, Moore or the other B006 names is documented, nor to B047 or B003. My research on infrastructure, regional growth and labour markets in economic history is far from macro-finance. I note that Lund colleague Tommy Andersson prefers B047, which is my first alternative, and that this is a collegial affiliation and not a candidate-related connection.
